content.thinking:
I'm figuring out the loft geometry for the body shape, considering using around 10 sides for a faceted low-poly look rather than fully smooth circles.

Now I'm planning out the color palette for skin, eyes, hair, and other features, then working through the skeleton structure, starting with the pelvis as the root spine joint and building out the spine chain positions.

Next I'm defining the neck and head joints, parenting them to the spine chain, and setting up explicit bone references for head attachments before moving into the body loft stations.

I'm working through the torso loft stations one by one, adjusting height and width at each z-position to get the rump, hip, and back proportions right—tweaking the pelvis station's y and height values so the back peak aligns better with the hip height rather than overshooting it.

Continuing through the belly, shoulder, and neck stations, I'm adjusting the belly's bulge and confirming the shoulder top hits the target height before moving to the neck-to-head transition and skull overlay. Then I check that the loft path and leg placement work together, making sure the leg tubes tuck inside the body silhouette at the hip width.

Now I'm defining the leg joint pivots — shoulder, elbow, and foot targets for front legs, then hip and foot targets for hind legs — checking the leg radius against belly width so the thighs bulge naturally without poking through. I'm sketching out the limb helper function signature and starting to wire up the leg chains to their parent spine joints.

Tapering the leg radius from thick at the shoulder down toward the foot, matching the chain endpoint to the foot cylinder's position.

Placing toenails at four angles around the front of each foot cylinder, using small cone shapes oriented outward with a dusty tan color, then adding a heel pad for extra detail.

For the ankle, I'm adding a thin horizontal torus ring to create a wrinkle fold effect, repeating this for each foot. I'm also planning a toe joint as a digit-role child bone near the front of the foot for aiming toe nails, then considering leg surface creases using the loop/sweep approach on the leg geometry.

Adding leg wrinkle loops...

Now working on the skull shape, placing station points for a loft from back of head to forehead. I'm checking proportions so the head top sits sensibly relative to shoulder height, adjusting the first station's position and dimensions accordingly.

Continuing to add more stations down toward the trunk root and front face, then setting the trunk's starting point and radius. I'm sketching forehead domes as squashed spheres, brow ridges, cheek bumps, and estimating eye placement based on the skull's interpolated half-width at that height.

For the eyes, I'm planning to use surface-based placement -- finding a point on the skull via azimuth/elevation around a center point, then building the eyelid as a small dark sphere, the eyeball with pupil, and lashes as a ring of spikes oriented by the surface normal at that hit point.

Now I'm adding a small flattened, squashed dark brown gland behind the eye with a tapered streak running down the cheek. For the ears, I'm figuring out root attachment coordinates on the skull surface and working out an outline that spans vertically so the ear bottom lands safely above the floor.

I'm computing the outer ear tip position with a 50° backward sweep angle, then checking clearance against the shoulder body's width at the same height to make sure the ear doesn't intersect the body at various points along its length.

Now I'm checking whether the flat ear plane clears the front leg, confirming enough gap at the point where the ear and leg are closest. I'm also setting the ear's thickness to taper from 0.03 at the tip to 0.06 at the root with a small bevel, and defining a faceted 12-corner outline for the ear shape using (u,v) coordinates.

Finishing the outline curve down to a sharp tip and back, checking it won't self-intersect, then deciding to add light smoothing while keeping the tip sharp. Now I'm sketching a custom paint function for the ear that shades the rim, inner pink surface with veins, and outer gray surface based on the normal direction after the ear's swing and flare transforms.

I realize my normal-direction test for distinguishing inner/outer faces is wrong since wall normals also have a significant z-component, so I need to discriminate using the thickness axis vector instead, computing it per-side and checking which direction corresponds to the inner-facing surface.

For the ear coloring, I'll add subtle vein-like darker patches using cellular noise, blend toward gray near the hinge area, and keep things simple rather than modeling a separate rim fold for the ear thickness.

Now I'm setting up the trunk as a chained body part off the head using a catmull-rom path with eight segments named trunk1 through trunk8, and defining a sweep radius function that tapers from a wide base down to a narrow tip while adding small ridge-like undulations along the length.

For the underside texture, lighter with fine ridges mimicking wrinkle rings. For the trunk tip, I'm adding a nostril opening with flattened geometry and a small forward-spiking cone for the "finger" lip, checking the path's end tangent to orient it correctly since the trunk curls inward and down near the tip.

Refining the trunk path to curl forward-down like a J at the end, so the nostril faces the right direction with a flat cap and dark ellipse disc placed along the tangent at the tip.

Positioning the jaw joint beneath the skull, aiming forward near the trunk base, with a frustum-shaped lower jaw box in a pinkish skin tone sized to sit just under the skull's bottom edge. I'm also considering adding a small pink mouth-interior box in the gap under the trunk base for a visible mouth slit.

Now I'm planning the tusk geometry, routing the bone path from a base inside the skull near the premaxilla outward and downward in a curved trajectory to form the characteristic tusk shape.

Total length comes to about 1.88, which checks out fine since the trunk stays near x=0 while the tusks curve outward around x=0.4, so there's no collision. For coloring I'm planning a darker sheath band near the base blending into the skin tone, then transitioning into an ivory gradient with subtle streaked noise running along the tusk's length.

For hair, I'm sketching bristle cards as small SVGs — three curved black strokes on a narrow canvas — to scatter across the forehead, head crown, chin, and tail.

I'm scattering these hair cards across the skull using surface sampling filtered to upward-facing normals, keeping them small and slightly leaning, drawn directly in a dark charcoal color rather than relying on greyscale tinting. Then I'm adding a denser tuft of similar cards at the tail tip joint.

For the tail itself, I'm plotting the path starting at the rump near the pelvis, but I'm noticing the round end-cap on the body loft would dome outward and push the rump surface further back than intended, so I need to adjust the cap style or starting position to avoid the tail overlapping into the body's extended rump geometry.

Still writing tail root code...

Still working out the hair strand geometry...

For dorsal texture I'm thinking of adding wrinkle rings around the body at the spine joints, like loops cutting across the torso to mimic elephant-style fold lines, keeping them targeted to the body loft so legs aren't affected.

I'll do asymmetric wrinkle arcs on both flanks with tapering radius sweeps for a natural crease look, and skip the belly wrinkles for simplicity. For legs, I'll add full ring creases plus knee caps, and scatter about 60 small hair cards sparsely over the body for subtle texture.

Now I'm writing the hide paint function: it blends a dark-to-light skin tone based on large-scale noise, darkens cell borders to simulate cracks, lightens the belly area, and adds dust coloring near the ground based on height and fine noise.

I also want pink blotches on the ears and face, blended in using noise thresholds weighted by a region mask so they only appear near the head/trunk. For the trunk itself I'm adding ridge-like grooves by taking a repeating fractional pattern and darkening where it dips below a threshold, plus some underside shading.

Now I'm layering in finer anatomical details — a wrinkled eye-ring using a small flattened sphere, an amber eye sphere with a tiny dark pupil offset slightly outward, a bulging sheath where the tusks meet the skin, and ear-root folds. I'm also adding a temple gland streak as a dark stain trailing down the cheek using a flattened sphere, plus some extra toe texturing.

I'm checking part counts — ears, eyes with lids and lashes, tusks, trunk, wrinkles, hair cards, tail hairs, and nails all add up to roughly 100-150 parts, which feels sufficient but I want to push for richer detail by scattering around 120 tiny flattened low-poly shards across the body and legs to mimic elephant skin plating, possibly as a merged geometry for efficiency.

I decide skipping the separate skin plates is better since paint cracks can handle that texture, and I'll skip extra dust/mud lumps too. Now I'm moving to the actual code: figuring out the limb import API, how `b.chain` accepts a path or polyline of points for smooth leg tubes, and how to structure the chain hierarchy with proper parenting.

Setting up imports and the leg geometry...

Testing slightly shorter leg lengths like 0.92 or 0.9 to get a small bend offset at the elbow for the front leg's pillar look.

I'm also sketching out the foot placement, storing leg references in a lookup object, and planning crease loops along the leg tubes for surface detailing.

For the body, I'm adding thin ring-shaped crease sweeps at fixed points along leg paths, then thinking through similar crease loops on the torso using frames oriented along the body axis.

The body loft keeps rings sparse via catmull interpolation through roughly 7 stations, giving a faceted look. I'm using sides=10 for the neck and skull too, then setting up the ear extrusion with a directional frame and bevel to shape its thickness.

Now I'm tapering the ear thickness from thin at bottom to thicker near the hinge, defining the ear joint parented to the head, and computing a tangent vector for painting the ear surface...

The paint logic distinguishes the ear's inner concave face (facing forward, toward the head) from the outer face using the surface normal's dot product with the tangent — the inner side gets pink coloring like a real elephant's ear front, while the outer side gets the gray mottled rim texture.

Still working out the ear surfacing...

Now I'm computing eye placement using the skull surface function, hitting it at specific azimuth/elevation angles on the left and right sides so eyes sit lower than the ears, then stamping flattened spheres for eyelid rings. I still need to handle jaw, trunk base, mouth, cheeks, and decide whether to add brow wrinkles above the eyes.

Adding forehead dome geometry, cheek bumps, and brow ridges, keeping the dome centered slightly lower on the skull so its top stays within the overall head bounds. I'm checking that the total body height from shoulder to head top lands in the realistic 3-3.5 range for an adult elephant, then thinking about naming parts and possibly adding scars.

Writing joint and chain definitions for neck, spine, and trunk...

Now I'm adding the jaw joint as a child of head, plus the frustum box geometry for the jaw shape, checking that its dimensions fit beneath the skull without clipping.

For the eyes, I'm using a surface query on the skull to find attachment points around a given center, placing small embedded spheres on both sides to form the eyeballs.

Skipping the highlight sphere as unnecessary complexity. Now I'm adding lashes using a ring arrangement around the eye rim, spiking outward in the tangent plane with a tilt that leans them toward the hit normal direction for a lifted look.

I'm sketching an SVG hair strand made of a few curved bristle paths for texture, planning to reuse a wider version with more strands for the tail tuft.

Reusing the single bristle shape, I'm scattering it as hair cards across the skull, back, chin, trunk top, and ear edges, varying their size, lean, bend, and flow with randomized placement and minimum distance. Then I'm working out the trunk groove pattern, dividing the trunk's 2.4m length into 22 rings for the periodic texture.

Realistic elephant trunk wrinkles run 3-5cm apart, so I'm settling on about 20 geometric ridges aligned with painted valley lines using a triangle wave function, darkening grooves where the wave fraction falls near the valley edges. I'm noting that sharp kinks in the radius sweep need extra ring density to render cleanly, which I'll verify in preview, then moving on to the foot geometry using a cylinder primitive.

For nails, I'm positioning them around the foot rim at specific angles for front and hind feet, using small cone-like cylinders aimed outward and slightly embedded into the foot, though I'm still working out the right scale and orientation so they read as flattened nail shapes rather than spikes.

I'll add an ankle fold using a flat torus positioned at the joint, colored darker skin tone, plus a separate toe joint bone per foot (toesFL, toesFR, toesHL, toesHR) parented to the wrist so nails attach to a distinct digit bone with unique names across all four limbs.

Now I'm counting up the total joint hierarchy - pelvis, spine, neck, head, jaw, trunk, ears, tail, legs, and toes come to around 39 joints, which seems reasonable. I'm naming the limb chains consistently (shoulder/elbow/wrist for front legs, hip/knee/ankle for hind legs) with L/R suffixes, setting contact points at ground level, and planning to use the chain's frame interpolation to place skin creases along each leg before adding sparse body hair cards and tail coloring.

I'm also working out texture resolution math -- given the elephant's surface area versus texel density, a 2048 atlas gives roughly 6mm detail, which should be fine for the paint cells despite the computational cost of the noise octaves across a million texels.
